Sixty-two people were evacuated from the nearby campground and the lower North Kaibab Trail in the aftermath.

The disaster marks the second time in just over a year that a historic structure at the Grand Canyon has been struck by natural disaster. In July 2025, a destructive wildfire tore through dense pine forest on the canyon's northern edge, destroying the historic Grand Canyon Lodge, the North Rim's only lodging. The National Weather Service said the late-August flash flooding near Phantom Ranch struck in the drainage below the burn scar that wildfire left behind, a connection that speaks to how one disaster can set the stage for the next.
A Closure That May Have Limited the Toll

One detail from the disaster stands out as a genuine, if grim, stroke of fortune. Phantom Ranch's hiker dormitories had been closed since early 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent infrastructure projects, with one men's dorm and one women's dorm scheduled to reopen September 1, just days after the flood hit. Had those bunkhouses been open and full at the time, park officials and reporting on the incident suggest considerably more hikers could have been caught in the rising water.
Assessing the Damage

The National Park Service is still cleaning up the campground and assessing damage to facilities and infrastructure across the area. The Interior Department told CNN it remains too soon to determine the full extent of the damage at Phantom Ranch itself. Construction at the ranch was historically carried out largely by foot and mule train, since no roads reach the canyon floor, a detail that underscores just how difficult both the original construction and any future rebuilding effort at the site genuinely are.
A Mascot That Survived One Disaster, Now Watching the Next

Amid the damage from last year's wildfire, one small piece of the park's history had a happier outcome. Brighty the Burro, a 600-pound bronze statue that had long greeted visitors at the Grand Canyon Lodge, was found damaged after the 2025 fire, but park officials chose to save the cherished mascot rather than let it be lost with the rest of the structure. The statue, modeled after a real burro who lived in the canyon in the early 20th century and, according to the Grand Canyon Historical Society, gave children rides and hauled water to a nearby summer camp in exchange for pancakes, is now being kept safe at the Grand Canyon Museum Collection facility, with no timeline yet set for its restoration or eventual return to the North Rim.
A Pattern Playing Out at National Parks Nationwide

The back-to-back disasters at one of America's most visited national parks are unfolding against a broader pattern of extreme weather intensifying at protected natural sites nationally, as reporting on the flooding has noted. The Grand Canyon's mile-deep landscape can look timeless to visitors, but the past thirteen months have delivered a stark reminder that its historic structures, many built decades before modern flood and fire risk assessments existed, remain genuinely vulnerable to the kind of compounding natural disasters climate scientists have warned are becoming more frequent and more severe across the American Southwest.

finance.title: Bond Traders Watch One Number as US Debt Fears Grow
finance.dek: Treasury yields near 4.8% as US debt tops $40 trillion — strategists warn of spillover risk to stocks and real estate, with $8.4T due by year-end.
finance.author: Emma Brooks
finance.metaDescription: The 10-year Treasury yield is nearing a critical 4.8% level as US debt tops $40 trillion, with strategists warning of ripple effects into stocks and real estate.

body.text: There's a number bond traders have started watching more closely than almost anything else in markets right now: 4.8%. That's the level the 10-year Treasury yield is approaching, according to Matt Maley, chief market strategist at Miller Tabak + Co., and it isn't an arbitrary line. It marks the high reached back in January 2025, and Maley warns a sustained move above it could create meaningful problems for other asset classes well beyond the bond market itself.

The pressure building underneath that number is genuinely substantial. Total US government debt has surpassed $40 trillion, and Maley estimates more than $8.4 trillion in government securities will need to be rolled over before the end of the year alone. Layer on top of that a corporate bond market doing brisk business of its own, September's high-grade corporate bond issuance could set an all-time record, according to Maley, with Goldman Sachs recently raising its full-year 2026 forecast for investment-grade issuance to $2.3 trillion, and the government now finds itself competing directly with corporations for a limited pool of investor capital within the same narrow window.
Why 'Fiscal Dominance' Is the Phrase Everyone's Using

Strategists tracking the bond market have increasingly reached for a specific term to describe what's happening: fiscal dominance, the idea that government borrowing needs have grown large enough to start driving interest rate dynamics on their own, regardless of what the Federal Reserve is doing with its own policy rate. Michael Chen, general manager at Noah ARK Hong Kong, has framed the structural pressure on Treasurys as steadily building under that dynamic, pushing investors to demand greater compensation for the risk of holding long-term US debt. He's responded by favoring gold and hard currency as structural hedges, while staying underweight on ultra-long-duration Treasurys and keeping exposure instead to quality equities and real assets, including AI-related physical infrastructure like power grids and data centers.

That skepticism isn't confined to one analyst. HSBC has turned more cautious on long-dated developed-market bonds broadly, raising its end-2026 forecast for the 10-year Treasury yield to 4.65% from an earlier 4.30% estimate, citing what the bank described as a higher structural floor under long-term yields and a more hawkish range of possible Fed policy outcomes than it had previously expected.
The Government Has Already Tried, and Struggled, to Bring Yields Down

It's not as though policymakers have been standing still. Verbal intervention from the Treasury Department and Secretary Scott Bessent has so far failed to produce the desired decline in rates, according to Maley's own assessment, and the Treasury has moved to more concrete action as well: on August 19, it announced that starting September 9, it would at least double the size of its long-dated security buybacks in an effort to actually pull yields lower rather than simply talking them down.

The scale of what's driving all this extends beyond any single data point. The 30-year Treasury bond yield closed at 5.27% on July 31, its highest mark since 2007, and net interest costs on the federal debt now consume 3.3% of the entire US economy in 2026, a figure the Peterson Foundation for Government Finance projects will climb to 4.6% within a decade. By 2047, on that same trajectory, net interest spending is projected to become the single largest category in the entire federal budget, ahead of defense, Social Security, or any other program.
What a Breach Above 4.8% Would Actually Mean

If the 10-year yield does push convincingly past 4.8%, strategists warn the effects wouldn't stay contained to the bond market. Assets that depend heavily on long-term cash flow projections, high-valuation growth stocks, commercial real estate, and various private-market assets, are considered particularly exposed to that kind of repricing, since higher long-term borrowing costs directly reduce the present value of cash flows expected many years into the future, the core math underlying how those assets get priced in the first place.

It's also worth noting this isn't purely an American story. Developed economies including Japan, the United Kingdom, and France are grappling with their own versions of the same fiscal pressure, part of a broader global shift where investors across multiple major bond markets are demanding higher compensation for holding long-term government debt, not just US Treasurys specifically.
The Underlying Problem That Isn't Going Away Soon

Maley has been direct about the limits of what near-term market moves can actually fix: even a temporary decline in yields wouldn't necessarily resolve the longer-term structural problem sitting underneath them. Ratings agencies have serially warned that US debt growth is unsustainable on its current trajectory, and bond market participants have taken note that an increasingly large share of the federal government's spending power now goes toward paying off yesterday's obligations rather than funding tomorrow's investments, a dynamic that's persisted even as policymakers have so far been unable to implement significant fiscal reforms to change the underlying trend.

finance.title: Uber Borrows in Euros for First Time Amid Big EU Deal
finance.dek: Uber hired five major banks for its first-ever euro bond sale, aimed at refinancing the €14.2B bridge loan behind its Delivery Hero takeover bid.
finance.author: Emma Brooks
finance.metaDescription: Uber hired five major banks for its first-ever euro bond offering, aimed at refinancing the €14.2 billion bridge loan behind its Delivery Hero takeover bid.

body.text: Uber Technologies is tapping the European debt markets for the very first time. The company has hired Goldman Sachs, BNP Paribas, BofA Securities, Deutsche Bank, and Morgan Stanley to arrange a series of fixed-income investor calls running September 7 through 8, laying the groundwork for a debut multi-tranche bond offering denominated entirely in euros, according to a person with knowledge of the deal.

A multi-tranche structure means Uber will issue bonds across several different maturities at once, spreading out its repayment schedule while giving investors with different time horizons, from those wanting shorter-term exposure to those comfortable locking in a longer holding period, options to actually participate. Specific tranche sizes, maturities, and pricing haven't been disclosed yet, which is standard at this early stage, just after banks have been formally mandated to run the deal.
Why This Specific Deal, and Why Now

The bond sale isn't a routine refinancing exercise, it's directly tied to one of the largest cross-border tech acquisitions currently in motion. Back in July, Uber entered into a €14.2 billion euro-denominated bridge credit agreement, financing built specifically to support the company's voluntary public takeover offer for Delivery Hero SE, the publicly traded German food delivery platform that operates across dozens of markets spanning Europe, Asia, and the Middle East.

Bridge loans are, by design, meant to be temporary, a short-term financing tool used to move quickly on a deal before being replaced with more permanent, longer-term financing. That's exactly the role this euro bond offering is meant to play: converting Uber's temporary bridge facility into the kind of settled, long-duration debt structure a company wants sitting on its balance sheet for years rather than months.
Solving a Currency Problem Along the Way

The euro-denominated structure solves a second problem for Uber beyond simply refinancing the bridge loan. Since earning an investment-grade credit rating, Uber has conducted multiple senior note offerings in US dollars, including bonds due in 2031 and 2035, using the proceeds largely to refinance older, higher-yielding debt. All of that borrowing activity, though, has been in dollars, even as a growing share of Uber's actual revenue, particularly post-Delivery Hero, comes in euros. That currency mismatch, earning revenue in one currency while carrying debt denominated in another, creates real financial risk from currency fluctuations alone. Issuing debt directly in euros closes that gap, functioning as a natural hedge rather than requiring Uber to layer on separate currency-hedging instruments to manage the mismatch.
A Long Way From Uber's Junk-Bond Days

This moment marks a genuine milestone in Uber's evolution as a corporate borrower. For years, the company carried sub-investment-grade, junk-rated debt, a direct reflection of its cash-burning growth phase, when profitability was more of an aspiration than an actual financial reality. Uber's very first bond sale as a public company, back when it was financing its acquisition of Dubai-based Careem, priced with a yield around 7.5% and carried ratings in the lowest tier of junk. This week's euro offering, by contrast, is happening from a position of investment-grade strength, with Uber able to access considerably more favorable terms than it could have commanded even a few years into its life as a public company.
The Bond Sale Isn't Happening in Isolation

The financing news lands the same week Uber announced roughly 3,300 job cuts, its largest round of layoffs since the pandemic, a combination that's put the company's stock squarely in investors' focus. Uber shares were trading around $75.70 as of early September, a level that market analysis firm GuruFocus characterized as sitting roughly 23.6% below its own proprietary GF Value estimate of $99.20, a gap that frames the stock as potentially undervalued relative to that particular model, assuming Uber can sustain its current operational momentum and manage the new euro-denominated debt responsibly.
What Happens Next

With investor calls running through September 8, pricing and final terms for the bond offering are expected to follow in short order once the roadshow wraps up. For a company that spent its early years as a public borrower paying steep yields to access debt markets at all, successfully placing a debut euro bond offering to help fund one of its largest acquisitions to date marks a genuinely different chapter, one where Uber's financing options increasingly resemble those of an established, investment-grade blue-chip company rather than the fast-growing, cash-burning startup it once was.

finance.title: Apple's $2,000 Bet: Why Wall Street Watches iPhone Launch
finance.dek: Tuesday's event debuts Apple's first foldable iPhone and tests new CEO John Ternus, with Morgan Stanley estimating $14B in added December-quarter revenue.
finance.author: Emma Brooks
finance.metaDescription: Apple's September 9 foldable iPhone launch, its first big event under new CEO John Ternus, could add $14 billion in quarterly revenue, Morgan Stanley says.

body.text: Apple holds its fall product event Tuesday at Apple Park, and for once, the anticipation genuinely matches the hype. The headline act is widely expected to be the company's first-ever foldable iPhone, described by Morgan Stanley analyst Erik Woodring as Apple's most consequential launch since the iPhone X, the device that redefined the entire smartphone category back in 2017. It's also the first major product event for John Ternus, who took over as Apple's CEO earlier this month, meaning Tuesday doubles as an early referendum on his product-first leadership approach.

The numbers riding on the launch are genuinely significant. Morgan Stanley estimates the foldable iPhone could contribute roughly $14 billion in December-quarter revenue on its own, with Woodring projecting Apple will build somewhere between 7 million and 8 million units in the second half of 2026, and as many as 20 million units across the device's full first product cycle.
A Genuinely Steep Price Tag

None of that demand is guaranteed, and price is the biggest wildcard hanging over the launch. Supply-chain research firm TrendForce projected the foldable could start between $2,099 and $2,299, while separate analyst estimates have put the broader range as high as $2,500. Layered on top of the foldable's premium pricing, Morgan Stanley expects some of the steepest like-for-like price increases in iPhone history across the standard lineup too, driven by rising NAND and DRAM memory costs that are expected to push Pro model prices more than $200 higher year-over-year, with TrendForce projecting overall price increases in the 10% to 20% range industry-wide.
What the Foldable Is Actually Betting On

Reporting on the device points to a book-style foldable design with an inner display in the 7.7- to 7.8-inch range and a folded thickness under 10mm, alongside Apple's next-generation A20 Pro chip, reportedly manufactured on TSMC's 2nm process, and a second-generation in-house C2 modem. The strategy reflects a broader industry bet: research firm IDC expects the global foldable smartphone market to grow 12.6% in 2026 and accelerate to 18% growth the following year, with Apple projected to capture as much as 40% of global foldable shipments by 2027 if the launch goes well.
Why Wall Street Is Split on the Stock

Apple shares head into Tuesday's event trading close to their average analyst price target, with the stock's consensus rating sitting at Moderate Buy across the 41 analysts who cover it, 21 with a Strong Buy rating, three Moderate Buy, thirteen Hold, and four with some form of sell rating. Estimates for where the stock could land immediately following the event diverge sharply: one analysis has floated a bull case around $400 against a bear case near $263.66, a genuinely wide spread that reflects just how much hinges on both the launch's reception and how markets read Apple's pricing power heading into the crucial holiday quarter.

At roughly 37 times forward earnings heading into the event, Apple stock isn't priced as an obvious bargain regardless of how Tuesday goes, meaning the launch functions less as a chance to reset an undervalued stock and more as confirmation, or a real challenge, to the premium valuation the market has already assigned it.
The Bigger Financial Picture Behind the Launch

Apple's underlying business heading into Tuesday remains genuinely strong on its own. iPhone revenue climbed 22% year-over-year to $54.3 billion in the June quarter, while total company revenue rose 16% to $109.4 billion, and management has guided for 9% to 11% growth in the September quarter with iPhone revenue growth in the mid-teens. That baseline strength is exactly why the foldable matters as more than a single product launch: after years of criticism that Apple's fall events lacked major form-factor upgrades, the foldable gives the company a genuine new growth catalyst rather than an incremental camera or chip refresh.
What Happens After Tuesday

For investors, the practical read heading into the event is a cautious one: Tuesday's launch is the opportunity, but the real test comes in the weeks after, once early sales data, reviews of the foldable's durability, and initial demand signals start rolling in. Whether Ternus can convert what Morgan Stanley calls Apple's biggest form-factor bet in nearly a decade into sustained revenue growth, or whether steep pricing dents demand more than analysts currently expect, is likely to shape how Wall Street values Apple stock well beyond just this single earnings cycle.

finance.title: All Eyes on the Fed: What to Expect From the Sept. 16 Decision
finance.dek: With inflation cooling but the committee divided, the Fed's September meeting brings both a rate decision and a fresh look at where the economy heads in 2027.
finance.author: Emma Brooks

body.text: Wall Street's biggest event of the month is now less than two weeks away. The Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee meets September 15 and 16, with a policy announcement due at 2:00 p.m. ET on the 16th, followed by a press conference from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh. Unlike a routine hold-or-move decision, this meeting also comes with an updated Summary of Economic Projections, the quarterly "dot plot" that gives markets their clearest view yet of where officials expect rates to land over the next few years.

The committee enters the meeting after holding its benchmark rate steady at 3.50% to 3.75% in July, a decision that passed on a divided 9-3 vote, with three officials pushing for a hike instead. Since then, the inflation picture has eased considerably. Headline consumer prices cooled to 3.5% in June, down sharply from 4.2% in May, largely thanks to a sizable pullback in energy costs, while core inflation, which strips out food and fuel, slipped to 2.6%. That cooling trend has fueled expectations that the Fed may finally be ready to pivot back toward cuts after keeping rates unchanged since December.
A Job Market That Complicates the Picture

Not everyone on the committee is convinced the fight against inflation is finished, and a surprisingly strong August jobs report has only added to the debate. Stronger-than-expected payroll growth, combined with rising oil prices and a stubborn Treasury yield curve, has left some economists wondering whether the Fed's next move could actually be a hike rather than a cut, a scenario that seemed unthinkable just a few months ago. That tension between a cooling inflation trend and a resilient labor market is exactly the kind of split decision that has defined Fed meetings for much of 2026.

For everyday borrowers and investors, the stakes are real. Mortgage rates, credit card APRs, and savings account yields have all been shaped by the Fed's cautious, data-dependent approach this year, and September's projections will offer the first real signal of how officials see 2027 shaping up. Whatever the committee decides, markets are bracing for volatility around the announcement, with traders parsing every word of Chair Warsh's press conference for clues about what comes next.

finance.title: Wall Street on Edge as Hot Jobs Report Scrambles Rate Cuts
finance.dek: A stronger-than-expected August payrolls report sent Treasury yields to multiyear highs and rattled stocks, complicating the Fed's path ahead of its pivotal September meeting.
finance.author: Emma Brooks

body.text: For weeks, investors had been pricing in a straightforward story: cooling inflation would give the Federal Reserve room to cut interest rates again this month. Then Friday's jobs report threw a wrench into that narrative. The U.S. economy added 162,000 jobs in August, triple what economists surveyed by Dow Jones had expected, while the unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%. Revisions to June and July also pushed both months higher, painting a labor market that looks far more resilient than Wall Street had assumed.

Markets didn't take the news well. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 272 points, the S&P 500 slid 0.4%, and Treasury yields jumped as traders recalculated the odds of a September rate cut. The benchmark 10-year yield touched levels not seen since late 2023 earlier in the week, and the 2-year yield, which tends to track Fed policy expectations most closely, hit its highest point since January 2025. For a market that has leaned heavily on hopes of cheaper borrowing costs, the reversal was a reminder that the path to lower rates is rarely a straight line.
A Market Still Chasing Records, Despite the Turbulence

Even with the recent bumps, 2026 has largely been a good year for stocks. Eight of the eleven S&P 500 sectors are in positive territory for the year, led by a red-hot energy sector that's up more than 40%, while both the Dow and S&P are on pace for back-to-back quarterly gains. But the rally has been uneven underneath the surface. Consumer-facing names like Nike have slumped to multi-decade lows, and travel and leisure stocks including Wynn Resorts and Carnival have also hit 52-week lows, even as healthcare and energy names notch fresh highs, a split that strategists say reflects growing unease about consumer spending heading into the holidays.

The next major test comes fast. With the Fed's rate decision landing September 16, this week's inflation data and any fresh commentary from Fed officials will be picked apart for clues about which way the committee leans. Some analysts now think a rate hike, not a cut, can't be ruled out if incoming data keeps running hot, a scenario that would have seemed far-fetched just a month ago. Until then, expect the kind of choppy, headline-driven trading that has defined markets for much of the back half of 2026.

sports.title: US Tennis Stars Reach US Open Quarterfinals in Historic Run
sports.dek: A record U.S. tennis run at the 2026 US Open continues as Shelton, Pegula and Tiafoe lead America's deepest quarterfinal push in more than 20 years.
sports.author: James Carter

body.text: It has been years since American tennis fans had this much to cheer about on their own turf. Heading into the second week of the 2026 US Open, ten U.S. players have punched their tickets to the round of 16, and five American men reached the fourth round for the first time since 1995. For a sport that has spent much of the last two decades searching for its next homegrown star, this year's tournament at the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center feels like a turning point.

The men's draw has been especially chaotic, with six of the top ten seeds already eliminated and several matches decided by the finest of margins. Through it all, the American contingent has kept finding a way to survive. Frances Tiafoe extended his unbeaten streak inside Louis Armstrong Stadium with a gritty three-set win over former finalist Daniil Medvedev, while eighth-seeded Ben Shelton cruised past Stefanos Tsitsipas to reach the quarterfinals for the second time in his career, both trips coming in New York.
Pegula and Shelton Set the Pace

On the women's side, third-seeded Jessica Pegula has looked just as composed, dropping only a handful of games on her way past Sorana Cirstea to reach her second straight Grand Slam quarterfinal. She's now chasing a return trip to the final after coming up short in 2024. Waiting for her next is fellow American Emma Navarro, a former US Open semifinalist who dispatched Anna Kalinskaya in straight sets, setting up an all-American showdown with plenty on the line.

For Shelton, the road ahead only gets tougher, with defending champion Carlos Alcaraz looming in the next round. Still, the 23-year-old has looked like a more complete player than the one who reached his first major final on this same court in 2023, and he's not shy about saying he believes this is the year an American man finally ends the tournament's long title drought. With home crowds behind them and a bracket that has already chewed up half the seeds, the US Open's second week promises to be one of the most compelling in recent memory.

sports.title: NFL Season Opens With Seahawks-Patriots Super Bowl LX Rematch
sports.dek: Defending champion Seahawks host Drake Maye and the Patriots in a Super Bowl LX rematch at Lumen Field, reopening February's title game rivalry.
sports.author: James Carter

body.text: Football is back, and the NFL couldn't have scripted a better way to bring it. The 2026 season opens Wednesday night at Lumen Field, where the Seattle Seahawks will raise their Super Bowl LX banner and immediately turn around to face the very team they beat to get it: the New England Patriots. It's only the third time in league history that the previous season's Super Bowl teams have met again in Week 1, and just the second time it's happened in the opener itself.

Kickoff is set for 8:20 p.m. ET, with NBC's Football Night in America starting the coverage an hour earlier. It's a Wednesday game rather than the usual Thursday slot, cleared to make room for the league's first-ever regular-season game in Melbourne, Australia, which follows the next night. History leans toward the champs: since 2004, teams that opened the season as defending Super Bowl winners have gone 16-5 in that game.
Darnold and Maye Renew Their Rivalry

Sam Darnold's remarkable turnaround season ended with a Super Bowl ring in Santa Clara back in February, and he'll get a shot to prove it wasn't a one-off in front of Seattle's home crowd. On the other sideline, Drake Maye enters his second full season as New England's starter looking sharper and more assured than the quarterback who struggled in that Super Bowl loss. Both teams built their identities on physical, disciplined defense, so points may be hard to come by early, with the turnover battle likely deciding who leaves Lumen Field happy.

Beyond the opener, this Week 1 slate is loaded with early statement games, including the Buccaneers at the Bengals and the Ravens traveling to Indianapolis on Sunday. But all eyes start with Seattle and New England, a fitting reminder that the road to Super Bowl LXI in February runs right back through the two teams that played for the last one.

sports.title: MLB Playoff Races Tighten as September Sprint Toward October Begins
sports.dek: MLB playoff races heat up with three division titles undecided and seven AL teams battling for Wild Card spots, all still below .500 with October approaching.
sports.author: James Carter

body.text: The calendar has flipped to September, and for most of Major League Baseball, that means one thing: crunch time. With roughly three weeks left before the regular season wraps up on September 27, the majority of the league is still fighting for its postseason life. Twenty-two of the 30 teams entered the stretch run either in a playoff spot or within striking distance of one, setting up one of the more chaotic finishes in recent memory.

The National League Central and West appear all but settled, with the Milwaukee Brewers and Los Angeles Dodgers cruising toward division titles. But nearly everything else remains a fight. In the NL East, Atlanta has opened a comfortable cushion over Philadelphia, though the Phillies have clawed back into postseason position after a rough start to the year and are now locked in a tight battle with the Chicago Cubs for the top NL Wild Card seed.
The AL Wild Card Chaos

Nowhere is the drama thicker than the American League Wild Card race, where seven teams entered the holiday weekend separated by just a handful of games, and remarkably, not one of them owned a winning record. Tampa Bay has managed to hold a modest division lead in the AL East over a resurgent Yankees club, while the White Sox and Astros are fending off the Guardians, Rangers and Mariners in their own division fights. Every series down the stretch carries added weight, with tiebreaker scenarios already shaping how front offices are approaching their final rotations.

The format hasn't made things any easier on the favorites, either. Since Major League Baseball introduced the best-of-three Wild Card round in 2022, the lower-seeded road team has actually won more often than not, a reminder that a hot week in late September can matter just as much as a great April. Whichever clubs stumble into October as the third seed in their league will get no home-field cushion and little margin for error, when the postseason field is finalized on September 27 and Wild Card Series play begins two days later.

sports.title: No. 1 Ohio State Faces No. 5 Texas as Underdogs in Austin
sports.dek: No. 1 Ohio State faces No. 5 Texas in Austin as underdogs, with both teams coming off big wins and College GameDay on hand for the marquee matchup.
sports.author: James Carter

body.text: One week into the college football season, the sport is already serving up its biggest game of September. Defending national champion Ohio State travels to Austin on Saturday night to face No. 5 Texas, a rematch of last year's College Football Playoff semifinal and the third straight season these two programs have squared off. Kickoff at DKR-Texas Memorial Stadium is set for 6:30 p.m. CT on ABC, with ESPN's College GameDay broadcasting live from campus all morning.

Both teams arrive having handled their openers with ease. Ohio State throttled Ball State 56-3 behind a huge night from receiver Jeremiah Smith, who caught eight passes for 151 yards and two touchdowns despite playing only in the first half, while quarterback Julian Sayin was nearly flawless, completing 21 of 25 passes for 320 yards and four total touchdowns. Texas answered with an even more lopsided 59-7 rout of Texas State, as quarterback Arch Manning bounced back from a rough start against the Buckeyes a year ago by throwing for 305 yards and four scores.
A Slim Line for a Program on the Rise

Despite carrying the No. 1 ranking and the reigning championship, Ohio State opened as a slight road underdog, with oddsmakers settling on Texas by 1.5 points after the line briefly touched 2.5. It's a testament to how quickly Manning and the Longhorns have built momentum at home, where Texas has now won its last two openers by a combined 47 points. Ohio State still holds the edge in the all-time series at 3-2, including a win over Texas in the Cotton Bowl semifinal last January, but Saturday marks the Buckeyes' first true road test of the season.

For a Texas program that has now hosted GameDay for three consecutive marquee matchups, this is the kind of stage the Longhorns have been building toward. A win would validate the preseason hype around Manning and vault Texas into the sport's clear top tier; a loss would simply reset the conversation heading into October. Either way, whichever team leaves Austin with the win will immediately become the favorite to represent their side of the bracket when the Playoff picture starts coming into focus later this fall.
